To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

race is associated with psychological distress, that the effect of race is particularly pronounced among people in low-income groups, that the effect is not entirely due to social class, and that the effect is suppressed in analyses that ignore the interaction between race and social class.

the effects of both social class and race on psychological distress are magnified when the interaction between them is considered, that this interaction has been overlooked by previous investigators, and that the true effect size for the race variable is much larger than has been previously reported.
the race and social class effects are not additive and that race differences in distress are particularly pronounced at low incomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of race, social class and psychological distress.
the effects of race on mental illness.
the effects of race on psychological distress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the race and social class variables are interactive in the prediction of psychological distress, that the effect of race is magnified in low social class groups, and that the effect of social class in high racial groups is magnified.
the race effect is real, but that it is moderated by social class.

the effect of race and social status on psychological distress is interactive, and that the effect of low social status is magnified and the effect of race is attenuated by the failure to consider this interaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
race and social class interact in a manner that magnifies the effect of the latter and that race differences are most pronounced among the poor.
the relationship between race and mental health is not simply a function of the effects of social class.
the relationship between race and mental health is more complex than is often assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social class and race are not interchangeable constructs, and that the relationship between them is not linear.
the relationship between social class and psychological distress is not the same for everyone; it varies depending on race.
race is a meaningful concept for understanding psychological distress.
